title: Chest drain: insertion and management
subtitle: Safe triangle, image guidance, and when not to

sources.title: British Thoracic Society Guideline for pleural disease
British Thoracic Society Clinical Statement on pleural procedures

sources.org: American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma
sources.title: Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) Student Course Manual

red_flags.text: Drain inserted below the nipple line or outside the safe triangle: risk of liver, spleen, diaphragm or heart injury.
A collapsed lung on the radiograph that could be a large bulla. Draining a bulla causes a bronchopleural fistula; get a CT first if unsure.
Complete white-out with the mediastinum pulled TOWARDS the white side: lobar collapse, not effusion. A drain will not help and may harm.
Sudden chest tightness, cough or hypoxia during drainage of a large effusion: re-expansion pulmonary oedema. Stop and clamp.
Fresh blood or a rapid rise in output from a drain: haemorrhage, which needs a surgical opinion now.
A bubbling drain that has been clamped. Clamping a drain with an air leak can produce a tension pneumothorax.

do_now.text: Use thoracic ultrasound to guide every drain for pleural fluid, either in real time or marking immediately before insertion with the patient in the same position.

Insert within the safe triangle: the anterior border of latissimus dorsi, the lateral border of pectoralis major, a line at the level of the nipple (fifth intercostal space), with the apex below the axilla.
Never use a trocar. Use a Seldinger small-bore drain or blunt dissection with a finger sweep for a large-bore drain.
Tension pneumothorax is decompressed on clinical grounds before any imaging, then a formal drain placed.

assess.text: Confirm the side against the imaging and the patient at the bedside, and mark it. Wrong-side drains still happen.

Indication and size: small-bore Seldinger drains are first-line for most pneumothoraces, effusions and pleural infection. Large-bore drains for trauma haemothorax and some cases of haemothorax or viscous collections.
Check coagulation and anticoagulant status in elective cases; do not delay an emergency drain for this.
Daily drain review: swinging, bubbling, draining, volume and character of fluid, insertion site and position on imaging.

investigate.text: Chest radiograph after insertion to confirm position and response.
Send pleural fluid for protein, LDH, pH, glucose, microscopy and culture, and cytology as indicated, at the time of insertion.
CT chest for a drain that is not working, an unexpected collection, suspected malposition or a suspected bulla.

resuscitate.text: Drain large effusions in a controlled manner and stop if the patient develops chest tightness, cough or vasovagal symptoms, to reduce re-expansion pulmonary oedema.
Keep the underwater seal bottle below the level of the chest at all times and never clamp a bubbling drain.
Adequate analgesia; give premedication or sedation only with appropriate monitoring.

definitive.text: Remove the drain when it has stopped bubbling and the lung is re-expanded for pneumothorax, or when fluid output has fallen and the effusion is drained for fluid indications.
Pleural infection: drain and give antibiotics; intrapleural fibrinolytic and DNase therapy, or surgery, for failure to drain.
Persistent air leak or failure of lung re-expansion: early discussion with respiratory and thoracic surgery rather than indefinite waiting.
Remove at end-expiration or during a Valsalva manoeuvre, and close the site.

escalate.text: Senior help when the safe triangle is difficult to define, the patient is obese, or ultrasound shows no safe window.
Thoracic surgery for haemothorax, persistent air leak, failed drainage of infection, or a drain in the wrong place.
Report every serious drain-related incident through the local reporting system.

notes: The safe triangle is safe because it keeps you above the diaphragm and lateral to the heart. The commonest serious errors happen below it.
Ultrasound before every fluid drain. A radiograph tells you there is fluid; ultrasound tells you where you can safely reach it.
The drain is only as safe as the ward that manages it: a clamped bubbling drain or a bottle on the bed is a tension pneumothorax waiting.
